task.prompt: Implement a thread-safe token-bucket rate limiter in `ratelimiter.py`: `RateLimiter(rate_per_sec, capacity)` with a method `try_acquire(n=1) -> bool` that grants tokens if available and refills continuously based on elapsed real time (not per-call ticks), allowing bursts up to `capacity`. It must be correct under heavy concurrency — many threads calling `try_acquire` at once must never together be granted more than `capacity + rate_per_sec * elapsed` tokens. Then write a stress test that spawns 50 threads hammering the limiter for ~1 second and asserts the total number of granted tokens stays within the theoretical maximum for that window. Show the test passing.
task.context: Empty scratch directory, plain Python 3, standard library only (threading, time). Single file. Note: use a monotonic clock and guard the check-then-decrement so it is not a data race.

task.prompt: Write `recurrence.py` with `expand_weekly(start_date, tz_name, weekday, hour, minute, count) -> list[str]` that returns the next `count` occurrences of a weekly event pinned to a fixed *local wall-clock* time (e.g. every Sunday 02:30 America/New_York), as timezone-aware ISO-8601 strings with correct UTC offsets across daylight-saving transitions. Handle the two DST corner cases explicitly: a local time that does not exist on the spring-forward day (e.g. 02:30 when clocks jump 02:00->03:00) and a local time that occurs twice on the fall-back day. Pick a defensible rule for each, document it in a comment, and include asserts that land an occurrence on both a spring-forward and a fall-back date to prove the offsets flip correctly (e.g. -05:00 vs -04:00).
task.context: Empty scratch directory, Python 3.9+ (use zoneinfo, stdlib only). Single file. The naive 'add 7 days in local time' approach silently produces wrong offsets or invalid times around DST — that is the point of the task.

task.prompt: Write `csvparse.py` with `parse_csv(text: str) -> list[list[str]]` implementing an RFC-4180-style CSV parser as an explicit character-by-character state machine — you may NOT use the `csv` module or a regex-splits-on-comma shortcut. It must correctly handle: quoted fields, doubled quotes (""") as a literal quote inside a quoted field, commas embedded inside quoted fields, and newlines (\n and \r\n) embedded inside quoted fields, plus a possible trailing newline. Include a deliberately nasty test string containing a quoted field with an embedded newline and an escaped quote, and assert the exact number of rows and the exact cell values — proving embedded newlines did NOT split a row.
task.context: Empty scratch directory, plain Python 3, standard library only but the `csv` module is off-limits. Single file. The classic failure is treating every raw newline as a row terminator.

task.prompt: Implement an `LFUCache` class in `lfu_cache.py` with `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` both amortized O(1), fixed `capacity`, evicting the least-frequently-used entry; when several entries share the minimum frequency, evict the least-recently-used among them. Do not scan all entries to find the victim — maintain frequency buckets with per-bucket recency so eviction is O(1). Add a demo that (a) forces an eviction where two keys tie on frequency and shows the LRU one is dropped, and (b) shows that a `get` bumps an entry's frequency so it survives a later eviction. State the O(1) reasoning in a comment.
task.context: Empty scratch directory, plain Python 3, standard library only. Single file. LFU is harder than LRU precisely because of the min-frequency + tie-break-by-recency invariant.

task.prompt: Write `money.py` with a `Money` type that stores amounts as integer minor units and is currency-aware about how many minor units a currency has (JPY=0, USD=2, BHD=3). Support parse-from-string / format-to-string, add, subtract, `split(n)` that divides an amount into n parts distributing the leftover minor units fairly so the parts sum back to the original *exactly* (no cents created or lost), and `times(rate)` that multiplies by a decimal rate and rounds to the currency's minor unit using banker's rounding (ROUND_HALF_EVEN). Never use binary floating point for money. Include asserts proving: `split` of USD 10.00 into 3 sums back to exactly 10.00; a JPY amount rejects/handles fractional yen; and a half-way multiplication rounds half-to-even (e.g. 0.125 -> 0.12, 0.135 -> 0.14 at 2 dp).
task.context: Empty scratch directory, plain Python 3, standard library only (use `decimal`, not float). Single file. Traps: float drift, wrong rounding mode, lost remainder cents, and assuming every currency has 2 decimals.

task.prompt: Write `kvstore.py`: a single-file, append-only, crash-safe key-value store. `set(k,v)`, `delete(k)`, and `get(k)` persist mutations to an append-only log file on disk; a fresh process replays the log on open to rebuild in-memory state. Implement `compact()` that rewrites the log to contain only currently-live keys, done atomically (write to a temp file, `fsync`, then `os.replace`) so that a crash at ANY point — including mid-compaction — never loses committed data and never leaves a corrupt log. Then write a test that: writes several keys, simulates a crash mid-compaction (create the temp file but kill before the atomic replace, in a child process via os.fork or subprocess), reopens the store, and asserts every committed key is still readable. Show it passing.
task.context: Empty scratch directory, plain Python 3, standard library only (os, tempfile, subprocess/fork). Single file plus its log on disk. The hard part is that atomicity must survive a crash between the temp write and the rename.

task.prompt: Write `semver.py` with `satisfies(version: str, range: str) -> bool` implementing npm-style semantic-version range matching: exact versions, caret `^1.2.3`, tilde `~1.2.3`, comparators `>=`/`>`/`<=`/`<`, hyphen ranges `1.2.3 - 2.3.4`, and `x`/`*` wildcards. Get the notorious edge rules right: caret on 0.x is special (`^0.2.3` allows patch bumps but NOT `0.3.0`, while `^1.2.3` allows any `1.y.z >= 1.2.3`), and pre-release versions (`1.2.3-beta.2`) compare by SemVer precedence and are only matched when the range explicitly names a pre-release on the same major.minor.patch (so `>=1.2.3` does NOT match `1.2.4-alpha`). Include asserts covering the 0.x caret case, a pre-release exclusion, and a pre-release inclusion.
task.context: Empty scratch directory, plain Python 3, standard library only. Single file. The spec is intentionally dense — the pre-release inclusion/exclusion rule and the 0.x caret carve-out are where most implementations quietly get it wrong.
